items.title: 68426_Nellie Lutcher oral history interview
items.q: Mr. Harts, who was the leader of the Imperial Orchestra and he said to my father, he said, 'Well, what about Nellie?' He said, 'Nellie plays well enough to play with us.'

ctx.x: Yeah, that's why I'm saying they had to wake me up. I would go to sleep. I would be sitting up there asleep and they would wake me up and say, 'Wake Sister Lutcher up. Wake little Sister Lutcher up and tell her it's time for collection.'

So they would wake me up and I would start playing, you know, and it was -- that was an awful lot of fun, and that's something that helped me an awful, awful lot. And then of course later on I -- they needed a pianist in the orchestra, because there was a piano player from Columbus, Ohio by the name of Al Freeman, and Al Freeman was a marvelous pianist, just marvelous, and he'd lived in Lake Charles for quite some time, and he decided to go back to his home town in Columbus, and he left, and of course they didn't…

it and he said, "Well, I think she can play well enough to play with us," you know, because sometimes at the house my dad and I would play, you know. He would be playing and I would play along with him. But my mother wasn't too keen on it. She didn't think too much of the idea. Well, of course it was a natural thing at that time, this was a biased thing, in thinking about religion and music, you know. And many people felt -- this was the general, not many, but it was the general feeling, somehow they looked down…
